steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on defending image classifiers against adversarial examples by focusing on a realistic threat model: transfer attacks from publicly available models. Explain why current ML-level defenses fall short, lay out the threat model, and introduce our defense with its headline results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- ML models are fragile against adversarial examples; progress on robustness has stalled
- Systems-level vs ML-level defenses
- Problems with current ML-level defenses
- Our approach: use systems-level defenses + TAPM threat model
- PubDef and results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Fragility
  - adversarial examples: small imperceptible change radically changes classification
  - lots of research on ML-based robustness methods; progress slowed, far short of practical needs
  - we articulate a new approach aimed at pragmatic improvements
- Two defense strategies
  - systems-level: secret weights, return only predicted class (no confidence scores), monitor use for anomalous patterns, etc.
  - inadequate alone: transfer attacks work without knowing weights
  - so research focuses on ML-level: more robust models via architectures and/or training methods
  - early progress with adversarial training, then slowed; no clear path to strong robustness in a deployable model
- Problems with ML-level defenses
  - (1) unacceptable hit to clean accuracy (accuracy when not under attack)
  - (2) unrealistic threat model, increasingly recognized
  - linked: attacker given excessive powers -> strong security too hard; robustness/accuracy trade-off -> any non-trivial robustness costs too much clean accuracy
- Our approach
  - slogan for a different approach
  - use all available systems-level defenses; threat model shaped by attacks systems-level defenses can't stop
  - transfer attacks from public models (TAPM; Fig. 1 (a)): attack a public model, hope it transfers to target
  - public models widely available (model zoos) -> easy to mount, important to defend
  - attacker doesn't know weights or training set, can't train own model, can't do query-based attacks with many queries
  - assumptions partly driven by what systems-level defenses prevent/mitigate
- PubDef (Fig. 1 (c))
  - training method secure against TAPM; attractive for deployment
  - clean accuracy close to undefended model
  - adversarial accuracy under transfer from public models: 88.6% CIFAR-10 (almost 20 points over previous defenses), 50.8% CIFAR-100 (18 points), 62.3% ImageNet (26 points)
  - not perfect, not for all scenarios; pragmatic, no major loss of clean accuracy, as hard as possible for attackers

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Current ML models are fragile. They are susceptible to adversarial examples, where a small imperceptible change to an image radically changes how it is classified. This has led to a lot of research on ML-based methods to improve robustness to adversarial attacks. Unfortunately, progress has slowed and has fallen far short of what is needed to protect systems in practice. In this paper we articulate a new approach that we hope will lead to pragmatic improvements in resistance to attacks.

There are two defense strategies in the literature: systems-level defenses and ML-level defenses. Systems-level defenses include controls like keeping the model weights secret, returning only the predicted class and not the confidence scores, monitoring the use of the model to detect anomalous patterns, etc. Unfortunately, systems-level defenses have proven inadequate on their own. For instance, transfer attacks can successfully attack a target model even without knowing its weights. So most research focuses on ML-level defenses, where we try to build models that are more robust against these attacks, for example through new architectures and/or training methods. Researchers made early progress on ML-level defenses when adversarial training was introduced, but since then progress has slowed a lot, and there is no clear path to strong adversarial robustness in any deployable model.

Current ML-level defenses have two major problems. First, they have an unacceptable negative impact on clean accuracy (the accuracy when not under attack). Second, they focus on a threat model that is more and more recognized to be unrealistic. These two problems are closely related. The prevailing academic threat models are unrealistic because they give the attacker excessive powers that are hard to realize in real life, which makes it too difficult to get strong security against these unrealistic attacks. And because there is a trade-off between adversarial robustness and clean accuracy, this means that getting any non-trivial adversarial robustness currently requires an unacceptable degradation of clean accuracy.

- Our approach: use all available systems-level defenses
  - threat model shaped by attacks systems-level defenses can't stop
  - transfer attacks from public models (TAPM; Fig. 1 (a)): attack a public model, hope it transfers
  - public models widely available (model zoos) -> easy to mount, important to defend
  - attacker doesn't know weights/training set, can't train own model or do many-query attacks
  - assumptions partly from what systems-level defenses prevent
- PubDef (Fig. 1 (c))
  - clean accuracy close to undefended model
  - adversarial accuracy: 88.6% CIFAR-10 (almost 20 points higher), 50.8% CIFAR-100 (18 points), 62.3% ImageNet (26 points)
  - not perfect; pragmatic, little clean accuracy loss, hard for attackers

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Current ML models are fragile. They are susceptible to adversarial examples, where a small imperceptible change to an image radically changes how it is classified. This has led to a lot of research on ML-based methods to improve robustness to adversarial attacks. Unfortunately, progress has slowed and has fallen far short of what is needed to protect systems in practice. In this paper we articulate a new approach that we hope will lead to pragmatic improvements in resistance to attacks.

There are two defense strategies in the literature: systems-level defenses and ML-level defenses. Systems-level defenses include controls like keeping the model weights secret, returning only the predicted class and not the confidence scores, monitoring the use of the model to detect anomalous patterns, etc. Unfortunately, systems-level defenses have proven inadequate on their own. For instance, transfer attacks can successfully attack a target model even without knowing its weights. So most research focuses on ML-level defenses, where we try to build models that are more robust against these attacks, for example through new architectures and/or training methods. Researchers made early progress on ML-level defenses when adversarial training was introduced, but since then progress has slowed a lot, and there is no clear path to strong adversarial robustness in any deployable model.

Current ML-level defenses have two major problems. First, they have an unacceptable negative impact on clean accuracy (the accuracy when not under attack). Second, they focus on a threat model that is more and more recognized to be unrealistic. These two problems are closely related. The prevailing academic threat models are unrealistic because they give the attacker excessive powers that are hard to realize in real life, which makes it too difficult to get strong security against these unrealistic attacks. And because there is a trade-off between adversarial robustness and clean accuracy, this means that getting any non-trivial adversarial robustness currently requires an unacceptable degradation of clean accuracy.

We advocate for a different approach. We propose using all available systems-level defenses, and we articulate a concrete threat model that is influenced by which attacks cannot be stopped by systems-level defenses. Specifically, the threat model we focus on is security against transfer attacks from public models (TAPM; Fig. 1 (a)). The TAPM threat model is about transfer attacks where the adversary starts with a publicly available model, attacks the public model, and then hopes that the attack will “transfer”, i.e., will also work against the target model. Public models are often widely available, e.g., in model zoos, so this kind of transfer attack is particularly easy to mount and therefore particularly important to defend against. Under the TAPM threat model, we assume the attacker knows neither the model weights nor the training set, and the attacker cannot train their own model or mount query-based attacks that query the target model many times. These assumptions are partly driven by which kinds of attacks can be prevented or mitigated by existing systems-level defenses.

Finally, we introduce PubDef (Fig. 1 (c)), a new method for training models that are secure against transfer attacks from public models. PubDef models are attractive for practical deployment. For instance, their clean accuracy is close to that of an undefended model, so there is little loss in performance when not under attack. Under attack (via transfer from public models), adversarial accuracy stays fairly high: 88.6% for CIFAR-10 (almost 20 points higher than any previous defense), 50.8% for CIFAR-100 (18 points higher), and 62.3% for ImageNet (26 points higher than any previous defense). Our defense is not perfect and is not appropriate in all scenarios, but we believe it is a pragmatic defense that can be deployed without major loss of clean accuracy, while making life as difficult as possible for attackers within that constraint.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Current ML models are fragile: they are susceptible to adversarial examples [1,2,3], where a small imperceptible change to an image radically changes its classification. This has stimulated a large body of research on ML-based methods to improve robustness to adversarial attacks. Unfortunately, progress has slowed and fallen far short of what is needed to protect systems in practice [4]. In this paper, we articulate a new approach that we hope will lead to pragmatic improvements in resistance to attacks.

In the literature, we can find two defense strategies: systems-level defenses and ML-level defenses. Systems-level defenses include controls such as keeping the model weights secret, returning only the predicted class and not confidence scores, monitoring use of the model to detect anomalous patterns, etc. Unfortunately, systems-level defenses have proven inadequate on their own: for instance, transfer attacks can successfully attack a target model even without knowledge of its weights. Therefore, most research focuses on ML-level defenses, which try to build models that are more robust against such attacks, for example through novel architectures and/or training methods. Researchers made early progress on ML-level defenses with the introduction of adversarial training [5], but progress has since slowed dramatically, and there is no clear path to achieving strong adversarial robustness in any deployable model.

Current ML-level defenses suffer from two major problems: first, they have an unacceptable negative impact on clean accuracy (accuracy when not under attack), and second, they focus on a threat model that is increasingly recognized to be unrealistic [6,7,4,8]. These problems are closely related: prevailing academic threat models are unrealistic because they grant the attacker excessive powers that are hard to realize in real life, making it too difficult to achieve strong security against such attacks. Given the existing trade-off between adversarial robustness and clean accuracy, this in turn means that achieving any non-trivial adversarial robustness currently requires unacceptable degradation of clean accuracy.

We advocate for a different approach, captured in slogan form as follows:

We propose using all available systems-level defenses, and we articulate a concrete threat model influenced by what attacks cannot be stopped by systems-level defenses. Specifically, we propose security against transfer attacks from public models (TAPM; Fig. 1 (a)) as the threat model we focus on. The TAPM threat model focuses on transfer attacks where the adversary starts with a publicly available model, attacks the public model, and then hopes that this attack will “transfer”, i.e., will also be effective against the target model. Because public models are often widely available, e.g., in model zoos, this kind of transfer attack is particularly easy to mount and thus particularly important to defend against. Under the TAPM threat model, we assume that neither the model weights nor the training set are known to the attacker, and that the attacker cannot train their own model or mount query-based attacks that query the target model many times. These assumptions are driven partly by what kinds of attacks can be prevented or mitigated by existing systems-level defenses.

Finally, we introduce PubDef (Fig. 1 (c)), a new method for training models that are secure against transfer attacks from public models. PubDef models are attractive for practical deployment. For instance, they achieve clean accuracy close to that of an undefended model, so there is little loss in performance when not under attack. Under attack (via transfer from public models), adversarial accuracy remains fairly high: 88.6% for CIFAR-10 (almost 20 points higher than any previous defense), 50.8% for CIFAR-100 (18 points higher), and 62.3% for ImageNet (26 points higher than any previous defense). While our defense is not perfect and is not appropriate in all scenarios, we believe it is a pragmatic defense that can be deployed without major loss of clean accuracy, while making life as difficult for attackers as possible within that constraint.
